oahu.intro: Oahu's remarkable trees spread well beyond Honolulu. Foster Botanical Garden holds the biggest group for one modest fee, among them a baobab, a Bodhi tree of the Bodh Gaya lineage and a kapok older than the garden. Moanalua Gardens keeps the Hitachi Tree under its own ticket. Almost everything else is free, including a run of giant banyans through Kapiolani Park, the widest more than 27 metres round, a kapok on King Street, a mango in Nuuanu that outgrew its banyan neighbours, a rainbow eucalyptus in Wahiawa and a library earpod on the North Shore.
oahu.meta_description: Oahu's remarkable trees: a Bodhi tree and a baobab in Foster Garden, the Hitachi Tree, and Kapiolani Park banyans more than 27 metres round.
oahu.question_meta: Oahu's oldest confirmed tree is a kapok planted around 1851 in Foster Botanical Garden, roughly 175 years old. Where it stands, and what else to see.
oahu.question_answer: Oahu's oldest documented tree is the Hillebrand Kapok in Foster Botanical Garden, planted around 1851 by the garden's founder, William Hillebrand, on what was then his own homestead. That makes it roughly 175 years old, older than the garden itself.
oahu.question_context: Foster Botanical Garden holds seven of the thirty trees on this page, and its own founding is younger than its oldest tree. William Hillebrand planted a kapok on his Honolulu homestead around 1851, decades before it became a public garden; it now stands about 27 metres tall. Two more carry documented dates, a Bodhi tree of the Bodh Gaya lineage given to Mary Foster in 1913 and a baobab planted in the 1930s. Most of the rest are free and undated. Six banyan entries stand in Kapiolani Park, from the zoo gate to Poni Moi Road, two of them more than 26 metres round in the city's register. Elsewhere in town are banyans at Thomas Square, Iolani Palace, the Moana hotel, the International Market Place and the Kuhio Beach hula mound; the Geometry Tree of Ala Moana Beach Park; a kapok at the Department of Agriculture; a mango and a monkeypod in Nuuanu Valley Park; three trees at UH Manoa; and two at Queen's Medical Center. Out of town, a rainbow eucalyptus opens the tour at Wahiawa Botanical Garden and an earpod shades the Waialua library. The Hitachi Tree at Moanalua Gardens is the one other paid visit.

faq_add.q: What are the biggest banyans in Kapiolani Park?
faq_add.a: By the city's exceptional trees register, the banyan on Paki Avenue across from the Diamond Head Tennis Center, 27.4 metres round, and the one on Poni Moi Road at the corner of the archery range, 26.5 metres. Those figures run around the whole mass of trunks and aerial roots, not a single stem. Both stand in the public park and are free.

faq_add.q: Are there remarkable trees on Oahu outside Honolulu?
faq_add.a: Two on this page. A rainbow eucalyptus 34 metres tall is the first stop on the self-guided tour of Wahiawa Botanical Garden, which is free, and an earpod that Honolulu Magazine dates to 1902 shades the parking lot of the Waialua Public Library on the North Shore. Both are a drive from Waikiki rather than a walk.

kauai.intro: Every tree on this list arrived with somebody. Monkeypod only reached Hawaii in the 1840s, and the two thickest on the island's register stand behind a shopkeeper's store and in the front yard of a missionary house. A governor's men planted him a banyan in the 1880s that now measures close to twenty metres round. A plantation owner emptied his leftover nursery stock along a mile of road and made a tunnel out of it. Koloa has an African baobab behind a church and an earpod outside a funeral home, and Allerton Garden's figs were in Jurassic Park.
kauai.meta_description: Kauai's remarkable trees all arrived with somebody: a governor's banyan twenty metres round, a mile of eucalyptus, and the figs of Jurassic Park.
kauai.question_meta: The Kanoa Banyan at Niumalu, planted for a governor of Kauai in the 1880s, is the island's oldest datable tree. Where it stands and what is near it.
kauai.question_answer: The oldest tree on Kauai that anybody can actually date is the Kanoa Banyan at Niumalu, planted for Paul P. Kanoa, governor of the island, at some point in his 1882 to 1886 term, which makes it about 140 years old. It stands roughly 84 feet east of Hulemanu Road on the way down to the Menehune Fishpond, and its trunk and root mass together measure close to twenty metres round, the largest figure recorded for any tree on Kauai in the state's exceptional trees register.
kauai.question_context: Kauai has no thousand-year-old trees, and the dates explain why: the island's designated trees are overwhelmingly species people carried here, and the oldest of them went into the ground during the sugar era. The Kanoa Banyan has the firmest window of any of them. The Garden Island, the local paper, records that it was planted by the men of Paul P. Kanoa, governor of Kauai from 1882 to 1886, in his honour, that it still flourishes at Niumalu, and that Kauai County declared it an exceptional tree in 1990 at the request of the family who owned the property by then. That puts it at roughly 140 years. One tree could in principle beat it and cannot prove it: the monkeypod at the Gulick-Rowell House in Waimea, which local tradition dates to 200 years, a figure that fails because monkeypod is generally recorded as arriving in Hawaii around 1847. The Wilcox Banyan at Nawiliwili is the documented runner-up, planted in 1895. The Allerton figs, the Koloa earpod and the Hongwanji monkeypods carry no published age at all.

faq_replace.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq_replace.a: All but one. They stand on public roads, in a church yard, in Old Koloa Town and on the grounds of a resort at Nawiliwili, and the Gulick-Rowell monkeypod in Waimea is in full view from Huakai Road while the house is closed for restoration. The exception is the Moreton Bay figs of Allerton Garden, seen only on the garden's paid guided tour, $65 for adults.

faq_add.q: Where are the Jurassic Park trees on Kauai?
faq_add.a: In Allerton Garden, in the Lawai Valley on the south shore. The Garden Island recorded that the 1992 film's raptor-egg scene was shot among the roots of one of the garden's Moreton Bay figs. You can only see them on the National Tropical Botanical Garden's guided tour, which leaves from the visitor centre on Lawai Road.

faq_add.q: Is the big tree outside the Koloa mortuary an earpod or a monkeypod?
faq_add.a: The state's exceptional trees register says earpod, and a 2007 letter from Kauai's mayor listing the county's exceptional trees called it a monkeypod. The two are close relatives and often confused. The seed pods are the thing to check: an earpod's coil round into the shape of an ear.

maui.intro: Maui's most famous tree is currently behind a fence. The Lahaina banyan, planted in 1873 and grown into sixteen trunks, came through the August 2023 fire that destroyed the town around it, and the park it stands in has been closed ever since, so you look at it from Front Street. The other four are elsewhere on the island and open to anyone: a monkeypod in a Wailuku churchyard, a fig outside a county building that was once the police station, a kiawe on the coast road to Olowalu, and two Norfolk Island pines at an arts centre in Makawao.
maui.meta_description: Maui's Lahaina banyan survived the 2023 fire and is still fenced off. Four more, in Wailuku, Makawao and on the coast road, are open to visit.
maui.question_meta: The Lahaina Banyan, planted 24 April 1873, is Maui's oldest dated tree. What survived the fire, what is fenced off, and four trees you can walk to.
maui.question_answer:
The oldest tree on this list is the Lahaina Banyan, planted on 24 April 1873 and so 153 years old, in Lahaina Banyan Court Park at the corner of Front Street and Canal Street. It is also the only one of the five with a documented planting date. An article says one of the Norfolk Island pines at Kaluanui in Makawao is believed to be over 150 years old, but gives no basis, so read the banyan as the oldest we can prove rather than the oldest tree on Maui.

One thing to know before driving there: the park has been closed since the August 2023 wildfire and a perimeter fence keeps visitors back from the tree and from the burned-out Old Lahaina Courthouse beside it. The tree is visible from the fence line and from Front Street. As of February 2026 a full arborist assessment was still pending and county officials hoped to reopen the park before the end of the year if it proved safe.
maui.question_context:
The banyan can be dated because its planting was an occasion. Sheriff William Owen Smith put it in on 24 April 1873, a seedling sent by missionaries in India, to mark fifty years since the first American Protestant mission in Lahaina, and somebody wrote the date down. Nothing like that exists for the other four trees on this page.

The record behind them explains why. Hawaii protects individual trees under Act 105 of 1975, and the exceptional trees register that results carries species, girth, height, condition and owner, but no age field at all. Where a newspaper or a local history has published a planting date there is an age to give; for these trees nobody has, and a girth figure on a fig or a monkeypod will not stand in for one.

The nearest thing is a belief. A Historic Hawaii Foundation article says one of the two Norfolk Island pines on the Kaluanui estate in Makawao is over 150 years old, with no basis given, and the estate's own history does not date them. If you know when any of these trees went in, tell us and we will add it.

See all five on the Maui page.

faq_replace.q: What is the oldest tree in Maui?
faq_replace.a: The Lahaina Banyan, planted on 24 April 1873, which makes it 153 years old. It is the only tree on this list with a documented planting date. One of the Norfolk Island pines at Kaluanui in Makawao is believed to be over 150 years old, but nobody has published a basis for that figure.

faq_replace.q: Which trees on Maui can I walk right up to?
faq_replace.a: Four of the five. The monkeypod at Ka'ahumanu Church and the fig at the Kalana Pakui Building are both on South High Street in Wailuku, a few minutes apart, and both are free. The kiawe stands beside Honoapi'ilani Highway near mile marker 11, on state land, and the register records it as visible from the street and reachable. The Norfolk Island pines stand on the grounds of the Hui No'eau arts centre in Makawao, free to walk during opening hours; ask at the front desk where they are.

faq_add.q: Where are Maui's biggest Norfolk Island pines?
faq_add.a: The Hui No'eau Visual Arts Center in Makawao says two of Maui's largest stand on its Kaluanui estate, among more than seventy specimen plants and trees. The grounds are free to walk; a $6 guidebook from the front desk and a $12 guided tour on Mondays and Wednesdays cover the plants.

hilo.intro: Three of these nine stand in one small park in downtown Hilo, and three more line Banyan Drive on the Waiakea Peninsula, the trees of Babe Ruth, Amelia Earhart and Franklin Roosevelt from the 1930s. Kalakaua Park holds a banyan planted in 1882, a Caribbean divi-divi and an endangered native palm. A tropical almond of about 206 years stands outside a church on Haili Street, a coconut palm on the Waiolama Canal recalls a grove an 1864 chant already sang about, and a banyan sprawls along the trail above Rainbow Falls.
hilo.meta_description: Nine trees in Hilo: an 1882 banyan, a kamani of about 206 years, and the Banyan Drive trees of Babe Ruth, Amelia Earhart and Franklin Roosevelt.
hilo.question_meta: Hilo's oldest tree is the kamani outside Haili Congregational Church, about 206 years. Its story, and the other remarkable trees around town.
hilo.question_answer:
The oldest tree in Hilo is the kamani at the corner of Haili Street and Ululani Street, on the pavement outside Haili Congregational Church. The Hawaii Tribune-Herald put its age at 194 years in 2014, which makes it about 206 now, so it was standing here before the church beside it and before Hilo was a town of any size. Hawaii's exceptional-tree register records it at 12.2 metres round and rates its condition good.

One caution about its name, because the register and the town disagree. The register files it as a False Kamani, Terminalia catappa, the tropical almond. Local usage, including that newspaper piece, drops the qualifier and calls it a kamani, which botanically means a different tree altogether, Calophyllum inophyllum. This page follows the register on the species and the newspaper on the age.

What makes it visible from across the street: Terminalia catappa throws its branches out in flat horizontal whorls that stack up the trunk, so it reads as a series of green plates rather than a dome, and its leaves turn red and drop in a place where almost nothing else changes colour.
hilo.question_context:
Hawaii protects trees in an unusual way and it shapes most of this page. Act 105 of 1975 lets each county designate individual specimens as exceptional trees, and the designation attaches to the tree rather than to the land, which is why the register names single trunks on street corners instead of woodland. The City and County of Honolulu publishes the database under a public-domain dedication, and it covers all four counties. It carries no age field, so every year given here comes from a newspaper or a local history, and its coordinates are rounded to about a kilometre, so every pin is marked approximate and each entry says what to look for on the ground.

The three Banyan Drive trees are a different record. They are dated by the visitors who planted or touched them between 1933 and 1935, Babe Ruth, Franklin Roosevelt and Amelia Earhart, and they are found by their brown wooden plaques, some of which have rotted or gone. See the full list of nine on the Hilo page.

faq_replace.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq_replace.a: Mostly. Three share Kalakaua Park in the middle of downtown, the kamani is a few minutes away on Haili Street, and the coconut palm is a short walk along the Waiolama Canal. Banyan Drive is about 1.5 kilometres from Kalakaua Park, some 20 minutes on foot, and the banyan at Rainbow Falls is about two kilometres out in the other direction.

Yes, all nine. Kalakaua Park is a public square open daily, the kamani stands on a public pavement, the coconut palm is inside the free Wailoa River State Recreation Area, Banyan Drive is a public road with a shoreline walk, and Wailuku River State Park is free and open from sunrise to sunset.

faq_replace.q: Why are the pins marked approximate?
faq_replace.a: Because the register's coordinates are rounded to roughly a kilometre and several trees in Kalakaua Park share one point between them. On Banyan Drive no source places the Earhart and Roosevelt trees on the loop at all, so those pins mark the road and the plaques are the way to find them. Marking any of these confirmed would be inventing a precision nobody has.

faq_add.q: Who planted the banyans on Banyan Drive in Hilo?
faq_add.a: Famous visitors, and about fifty of their plaqued banyans remain. Babe Ruth planted one on 28 October 1933, his first day in Hilo, a week after Cecil B. DeMille planted his. Amelia Earhart planted one in 1935, days before her solo flight from Honolulu to Oakland. Franklin Roosevelt, visiting on 25 July 1934, touched his and threw dirt on its base without leaving his car.

hawaii.oldest_tree_reason: Documented planting: Big Island Now (2022) says Queen Kapiolani planted it in the 1880s, Images of Old Hawaii says 1882; no Kalopa tree has any age. haw_008's 1906 date is a transplant, not a planting.
hawaii.intro: Six of these eight trees stand on one short loop trail in Kalopa State Recreation Area on the Hamakua coast, part of one of the last old growth native forest stands on the Big Island, among them a koa 3.66 metres round, an oversized hame and two ohi'a lehua holding the canopy. The other two are banyans on the Kona waterfront, grown from cuttings of the Iolani Palace banyan that Queen Kapiolani brought to Kailua in the 1880s, one on the lawn of Hulihee Palace and one at the entrance to Kailua Pier.
hawaii.meta_description: Eight Big Island trees: six on one Kalopa trail, including an old growth koa, and two Kona banyans from Queen Kapiolani's 1880s cuttings.
hawaii.question_meta: The Royal Banyan at Hulihee Palace, planted by Queen Kapiolani in the 1880s, is the oldest dated tree here. Its story, and the Kalopa trees.
hawaii.question_answer: The oldest dated tree on this page is the Royal Banyan on the front lawn of Hulihee Palace in Kailua-Kona. Big Island Now reports that Queen Kapiolani planted it in the 1880s from a cutting of the Iolani Palace banyan in Honolulu, and Images of Old Hawaii puts the year at 1882, so it is somewhere between about 136 and 146 years old. Its sibling at Kailua Pier came from the same royal cuttings but was transplanted in 1906, which dates its move rather than its age. The six native trees on the Kalopa Nature Trail have no documented age at all. The Larger Ohi'a Lehua has the biggest trunk there, 4.39 metres round, which makes it the largest of the six rather than provably the oldest. If you know the age of any of these trees, tell us and it goes on the page.
hawaii.question_context:
Two kinds of record meet on this page. The Kona banyans are dated by history. Two local sources agree that Queen Kapiolani brought banyan cuttings from Iolani Palace to Kona in the 1880s, one planted at Hulihee Palace and another transplanted to Kailua Pier in 1906, and the Daughters of Hawaii, who have cared for the palace since 1925, still pay for the Royal Banyan's upkeep.

The Kalopa trees are dated by nothing. Hawaii's Act 105 of 1975 lets each county designate individual specimens as exceptional trees, and the resulting register records girth and condition but carries no age field. Three of its height figures for Kalopa (a 184-foot koa, a 170-foot hame, an 84-foot kopiko 'ula) do not hold up against how tall those species grow anywhere else, so no heights appear here. Its coordinates are rounded to about a kilometre, so all six Kalopa trees are pinned at the park, where the 0.7-mile loop starts. What is solid is the girth, and the forest. Kalopa protects roughly a hundred acres of old growth native Hawaiian forest, one of the more intact stands left on the island.

faq_replace.q: What is the oldest tree in Hawaii's Kalopa cluster?
faq_replace.new_q: What is the oldest tree on the Big Island page?
faq_replace.a: The Royal Banyan at Hulihee Palace in Kailua-Kona, planted by Queen Kapiolani in the 1880s from a cutting of the Iolani Palace banyan, so about 136 to 146 years old. None of the six Kalopa trees has been dated; the Larger Ohi'a Lehua has the biggest trunk there, 4.39 metres round.

faq_replace.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq_replace.a: Not in one. The six Kalopa trees share the Kalopa Nature Trail, a marked 0.7-mile loop through Kalopa State Recreation Area on the Hamakua coast. The two banyans are on the other side of the island in Kailua-Kona, about seven minutes apart on foot along Ali'i Drive.

Yes, to see. Kalopa State Recreation Area is a free day-use park, open 7am to 8pm daily, with free parking near the trailhead. The Kailua Pier banyan stands on the public waterfront and the Royal Banyan is in full view from Ali'i Drive; only the interior of Hulihee Palace is ticketed.

faq_replace.q: Why are the pins marked approximate?
faq_replace.a: Because the state register rounds its coordinates to about a kilometre and all six Kalopa entries share one point, so they are pinned at the park. The two Kona banyans are pinned at the palace and the pier, not at the trunks. Marking any of them confirmed would be inventing a precision nobody has, so each entry describes what to look for instead.

faq_add.q: Where did the banyans in Kailua-Kona come from?
faq_add.a: From Honolulu. Local histories record that Queen Kapiolani brought cuttings of the Iolani Palace banyan to Kona in the 1880s. One became the Royal Banyan on the lawn of Hulihee Palace; another was transplanted beside Kailua Pier in 1906, where the village's free historic walking tour now begins.
